intro.headline: January 2021: Madrid under the snow
paragraphs: In early January 2021 storm Filomena brought Madrid its heaviest snowfall in about 50 years. Streets, roads and the airport closed, cars were stuck in the snow, and the city was paralysed for days.
When the storm passed, the sky cleared and a cold wave followed. The snow froze into ice, and many trees in the city broke under its weight.

Pictures of a white Madrid travelled around the world, and some people asked: if it can snow like this, is the planet really warming? A good detective does not answer with one picture. In this case file you will compare January 2021 with every other January since 1980, and then decide for yourself.
intro.question: If Madrid had its biggest snowfall in half a century, does that mean it is not warming?

steps.title: A wave that repeats
steps.text: This line is a time series of air temperature in Madrid: one point per month, from January 1980 to September 2026. Each point is the average temperature of that month, in °C, over the square of land that contains the city. The line makes a wave: warm summers, cold winters, every year. The marked point is January 2021, the month of Filomena. Data: NASA MERRA-2.

question.prompt: Where do the lowest points of each yearly wave fall?

options.feedback: Right: every year the line dips in winter, like January 2021.
Look at the marked point, January 2021. Is it near the top of the wave or near the bottom?

options.text: There is no pattern: the lows fall in random months
options.feedback: Follow the line across a few years. Do the dips come at the same time each year, or at random?

steps.takeaway: The seasons repeat every year, so January 2021 must be compared with other Januaries, not with July.

steps.title: Only the Januaries
steps.text: Here is a different way to read the same data: keep only one month of each year. Each point is one January, from 1980 to 2026, so 47 points in all. Now every point is compared with its own kind, and the summer-winter wave is gone. This is the detective's trick for a case like this one: compare like with like. The marked point is January 2021.

question.prompt: How does January 2021 compare with the other Januaries?

options.text: It is one of the coldest, but not the coldest
options.feedback: Yes: at about 2.2 °C it is the 4th coldest of 47 Januaries.

options.text: It is the coldest January in the record
options.feedback: Look for points lower than the marked one. Are there any Januaries below January 2021?

options.text: It is a normal, middle-of-the-pack January
options.feedback: Count how many points sit below the marked one, and how many sit above it. Is it really in the middle?

steps.takeaway: January 2021 was a very cold January, but colder ones happened before.

steps.title: Coldest and warmest Januaries
steps.text: The three coldest Januaries here are 1992, 1985 and 2000, all around 1.2 to 1.4 °C. January 2021 comes next, at about 2.2 °C. The three warmest are 2016, 2024 and 2008, at about 5.4 to 5.8 °C. A normal January in Madrid is about 3.5 °C. So one January can be more than 4 °C warmer or colder than another: that is the weather changing from year to year.

question.prompt: Where do the two warmest Januaries, 2016 and 2024, sit on the time axis?

options.text: In the last ten years of the record
options.feedback: Correct: the two warmest Januaries are both recent.
Find the labels 2016 and 2024 on the chart. Are they on the left side or on the right side?

options.text: Right next to January 2021, with no time between them
options.feedback: Look at the gaps between the labelled points. How many years are there between 2016, 2021 and 2024?

steps.takeaway: A record-cold month and record-warm months can sit side by side in the same years.

steps.title: A trend with only 47 points
steps.text: The straight line is the trend of the Januaries: about +0.2 °C every 10 years. But with only 47 points that jump by several degrees, the line is hard to pin down. The p-value is the chance of seeing a slope this big if nothing were really changing. Here p = 0.069, just above the usual 0.05 limit, and the 95% confidence range, -0.02 to +0.46 °C per decade, includes zero.

question.prompt: With p = 0.069, what can the detective say about the Januaries alone?

options.text: The line tilts up, but on their own the Januaries do not prove a trend
options.feedback: Well done: an upward slope that is not significant is still a valid result.

options.text: Januaries are clearly and significantly warming
options.feedback: A trend is called significant only when p is below 0.05. Is 0.069 below 0.05?

options.text: Januaries are getting colder, as Filomena shows
options.feedback: Follow the trend line from the left edge to the right edge. Does it go down or up?

steps.takeaway: Fewer points and big jumps make a trend harder to prove; not proven is not the same as no change.

steps.title: Weather and climate
steps.text: Now all 561 months, each compared with its normal value for that month (an anomaly). With twelve times more points, the trend is clear: about +0.37 °C every 10 years, about 1.7 °C over the whole period. Here p < 0.001 and the confidence range, +0.26 to +0.49 °C per decade, is all above zero. Weather is what happens in one month; climate is the long-term picture.

question.prompt: Where is January 2021 compared with the trend line?

options.text: Below it: a cold month inside a series that is warming
options.feedback: Exactly: one cold month does not stop the line from rising.

options.text: Above it: January 2021 was a warm month
options.feedback: Find the marked point and the straight line at the same date. Which one is higher?

options.text: It pulls the trend line down, so the series is cooling
options.feedback: Follow the trend line from left to right. Does it go down after 2021, or keep going up?

steps.takeaway: One cold month is weather; a rise over decades is climate.

steps.title: Where did the snow come from?
steps.text: Snow needs two things: cold air and moisture. This chart shows January precipitation in Madrid from 1998 to 2025, with snow counted as the water it melts into. Data: NASA GPM IMERG. January 2021 had about 1.9 mm/day, a little more than a normal January (about 1.6). The trend line has p = 0.40: no clear trend in January rain or snow.

question.prompt: Was January 2021 the wettest January in this record?

options.text: No, several Januaries were wetter, such as 2001
options.feedback: Correct: the snow was rare because it came with cold air, not because the month was record wet.

options.text: Yes, it is the highest point
options.feedback: Compare the January 2021 point with the one labelled 2001. Which one is taller?

options.text: No, it was the driest January
options.feedback: Look at how many points sit below January 2021. Is it at the very bottom?

steps.takeaway: A big snowfall needs moisture and cold together; neither has to be a record on its own.

conclusion.prompt: If Madrid had its biggest snowfall in half a century, does that mean it is not warming? Write your conclusion using what the charts showed you.
conclusion.placeholder: Looking at the temperature data for Madrid from 1980 to 2026, I think...

by_variable.T2M: Air temperature in Madrid (January 1980 to September 2026) rises clearly: about +0.37 °C per decade (95% range +0.26 to +0.49 °C per decade), p < 0.001, about 1.7 °C over the whole period. The 47 Januaries alone tilt up too (about +0.2 °C per decade), but with p = 0.069 that slope is not significant on its own. January 2021 was the 4th coldest January since 1980.
by_variable.PRECIP: January precipitation in Madrid (1998 to 2025) shows no significant trend (p = 0.40), and the full monthly series shows none either (p = 0.79). January 2021 was a little wetter than a normal January, but far from the wettest.

reveal.lesson: A very cold month is weather; climate is the picture over decades. Madrid is warming clearly, and a rare snowstorm does not contradict that. Comparing a month only with the same month in other years is a fair test, but it leaves fewer points, so a real change can be harder to prove: a non-significant result means the evidence is not strong enough, not that nothing is changing.
